title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Visualising Uncertainty with ggplot2

Computing Summary Statistics

my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n=n(),
    mean=mean(MATHS),
    sd=sd(MATHS)
    ) %>%
  mutate(se=sd/sqrt(n-1))



Standard Error Bars

The PlotThe Code














ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=RACE, 
        ymin=mean-se, 
        ymax=mean+se), 
    width=0.2, 
    colour="black", 
    alpha=0.9, 
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x=RACE, 
                 y=mean), 
             stat="identity", 
             color="red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha=1) +
  ggtitle("Standard error of mean maths score by race")






95% Confidence Interval

The PlotThe Code














ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=reorder(RACE, -mean), 
        ymin=mean-1.96*se, 
        ymax=mean+1.96*se), 
    width=0.2, 
    colour="black", 
    alpha=0.9, 
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x=RACE, 
                 y=mean), 
             stat="identity", 
             color="red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha=1) +
  labs(x = "Maths score",
       title = "95% confidence interval of mean maths score by race")






Interactive Error Bars: 99% Confidence Interval

The PlotThe Code





















shared_df = SharedData$new(my_sum)

bscols(widths = c(4,8),
       ggplotly((ggplot(shared_df) +
                   geom_errorbar(aes(
                     x=reorder(RACE, -mean),
                     ymin=mean-2.58*se, 
                     ymax=mean+2.58*se), 
                     width=0.2, 
                     colour="black", 
                     alpha=0.9, 
                     size=0.5) +
                   geom_point(aes(
                     x=RACE, 
                     y=mean, 
                     text = paste("Race:", `RACE`, 
                                  "<br>N:", `n`,
                                  "<br>Avg. Scores:", round(mean, digits = 2),
                                  "<br>95% CI:[", 
                                  round((mean-2.58*se), digits = 2), ",",
                                  round((mean+2.58*se), digits = 2),"]")),
                     stat="identity", 
                     color="red", 
                     size = 1.5, 
                     alpha=1) + 
                   xlab("Race") + 
                   ylab("Average Scores") + 
                   theme_minimal() + 
                   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
                     angle = 45, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1)) +
                   ggtitle("99% Confidence interval of average maths scores by race")), 
                tooltip = "text"), 
       DT::datatable(shared_df, 
                     rownames = FALSE, 
                     class="compact", 
                     width="100%", 
                     options = list(pageLength = 10,
                                    scrollX=T), 
                     colnames = c("No. of pupils", 
                                  "Avg Scores",
                                  "Std Dev",
                                  "Std Error")) %>%
         formatRound(columns=c('mean', 'sd', 'se'),
                     digits=2))

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Funnel Plot with ggplot2

Computing Derived Fields

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)



Computing Confidence Interval Limits

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq))

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
  if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Motor vehicle insurance is one of the largest lines of non-life (property & casualty) insurance globally. According to Swiss Re’s sigma research, non-life insurers face two fundamental challenges: maintaining profitability (ensuring premiums collected exceed claims paid) and managing volatility (the unpredictable nature of claim occurrences and severities).
This exercise analyses a detailed microdata portfolio from a Spanish motor insurance company, covering 354,140 policy transactions from January 2022 to December 2024 across 47 variables. The dataset captures policy characteristics, driver and vehicle attributes, premiums charged, and claims experience.



Using Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) methods and ggplot2 visualisations, this exercise explores:

Univariate distributions of all numerical and categorical variables
Bivariate relationships to statistically identify factors influencing profitability and volatility




Two derived metrics guide the analysis throughout:

Loss Ratio = total_incurred / total_premium — the primary measure of profitability. A loss ratio below 1 indicates the insurer collected more in premiums than it paid in claims.
Claim Frequency = total_claims / total_exposure — measures how often claims occur per policy year, a key driver of volatility.
Claim Severity = total_incurred / total_claims (where claims > 0) — the average cost per claim.

3 EDA 1: Univariate Analysis — Categorical Variables

3.1 Distribution of Policy Type


Show the code
p1 <- insurance |>
  count(policy_type) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%")),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", direction = -1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Policy Type",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

p1









Observation: The CC (Third-party + multiple coverages) policy type dominates the portfolio at over 60%, followed by COMP_E (comprehensive with excess) at around 22%. The basic TP (third-party only) policies are rare at under 1%, suggesting this portfolio skews toward customers who elect broader coverage. The near-absence of basic TP policies may indicate a relatively affluent customer base or a deliberate underwriting strategy targeting higher-coverage segments.



3.2 Distribution of Policy Status


Show the code
p2 <- insurance |>
  count(policy_status) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_status, y = n, fill = policy_status)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%\n(", comma(n), ")")),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Active" = "#2196F3", "Cancelled" = "#EF5350")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Policy Status",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

p2









Observation: Approximately 85% of policies are active and 15% cancelled. The cancellation rate of 15% is not negligible and warrants attention — policies cancelled mid-term reduce premium income and may signal adverse selection if higher-risk customers are disproportionately cancelling after claims.



3.3 Distribution of Business Type, Payment Frequency, and Bonus Score


Show the code
plot_cat <- function(data, var, title, palette = "Set2") {
  data |>
    count({{ var }}) |>
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
           var_col = fct_reorder({{ var }}, n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = var_col, y = n, fill = var_col)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%")),
              hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = palette) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Count") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}

p4 <- plot_cat(insurance, payment_frequency, "Payment Frequency")
p5 <- plot_cat(insurance, bonus_score, "Bonus Score")

p3 | p4 | p5









Observation: Portfolio renewals (62%) substantially outnumber new business (38%), consistent with a stable, mature book. Annual payment is overwhelmingly preferred (78%), likely reflecting discounts offered for upfront payment. The bonus score distribution is highly skewed toward “Good” (98%), indicating the portfolio is dominated by low-risk, experienced drivers with no recent claims history — a positive signal for profitability but also a potential limitation for analysing the “Bad” segment due to its very small size.



3.4 Distribution of Geographic Variables

Observation: Inland municipalities account for the majority (54%) with coastal at 36% and island at 10%, which broadly reflects Spain’s population distribution. Urban and rural circulation areas are nearly evenly split (51% vs 49%), suggesting good geographic diversity. Diesel vehicles dominate at 62%, though this may shift in future years as newer petrol and electric vehicles gain market share.

Vehicle age is right-skewed with a concentration of older vehicles (15–35 years), which is noteworthy as older vehicles are more likely to be total losses in accidents. Vehicle values are right-skewed with the majority clustering between €15,000–€40,000, but with a long tail of high-value vehicles exceeding €100,000 that could significantly impact claim severity.

On the log scale, the distribution becomes more symmetric, centred around €300–€400, which is typical for Spanish motor insurance. 6 EDA 4: Bivariate Analysis — Factors Affecting Profitability

6.1 Loss Ratio by Policy Type


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0, loss_ratio <= 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio, y = policy_type, fill = policy_type)) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
    alpha = 0.7,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio Distribution by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Vertical lines show Q1, Median, Q3. Red dashed = break-even",
       x = "Loss Ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Loss ratio distributions vary markedly across policy types. Comprehensive policies (COMP_E and COMP_N) show higher median loss ratios compared to basic coverage types, reflecting the broader coverage they provide. The TP and TPG policies have the lowest median loss ratios but also the smallest sample sizes. The long right tails are consistent across all policy types, driven by large individual claims.



6.2 Loss Ratio by Bonus Score


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0, loss_ratio <= 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bonus_score, y = loss_ratio, fill = bonus_score)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Good" = "#66BB6A", 
                                "Neutral" = "#FFA726", 
                                "Bad" = "#EF5350")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio by Bonus Score",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = break-even (LR = 1)",
       x = "Bonus Score", y = "Loss Ratio") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Policyholders with a “Bad” bonus score (poor claims history) exhibit substantially higher median loss ratios compared to “Good” and “Neutral” policyholders, confirming that the bonus-malus system successfully identifies high-risk customers. The “Bad” group also shows greater variance, contributing disproportionately to portfolio volatility. This validates the bonus score as an effective risk-tiering mechanism.



6.3 Claim Frequency by Driver Age Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(driver_age,
                          breaks = c(18, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 100),
                          labels = c("19-25", "26-35", "36-45", 
                                     "46-55", "56-65", "66+"),
                          right = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(
    mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency),
    median_freq = median(claim_frequency),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = mean_freq)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#42A5F5") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Driver Age Group",
       x = "Driver Age Group", y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency is highest for the youngest driver age group (19–25), consistent with actuarial research on inexperienced drivers. Frequency gradually decreases for middle-aged drivers (35–55) and slightly increases again for older drivers (65+), forming a characteristic U-shape. This pattern justifies age-based premium differentiation and explains why very young drivers are relatively absent from this portfolio.



6.4 Loss Ratio by Vehicle Age Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0, loss_ratio <= 5) |>
  mutate(veh_age_group = cut(vehicle_age,
                              breaks = c(-1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 60),
                              labels = c("0-5", "6-10", "11-15", 
                                         "16-20", "21-30", "31+"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = veh_age_group, y = loss_ratio, fill = veh_age_group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio by Vehicle Age Group",
       x = "Vehicle Age Group (years)", y = "Loss Ratio") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Newer vehicles (0–5 years) tend to have higher loss ratios, possibly driven by higher repair costs or higher declared values resulting in larger incurred amounts when accidents occur. The loss ratio distributions are broadly similar across vehicle age groups but with greater spread in newer vehicles, suggesting they are a key source of volatility. Very old vehicles (31+ years) show lower median loss ratios, possibly because they carry lower insured values.



6.5 Claim Severity by Policy Type


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_severity), total_claims > 0) |>
  filter(claim_severity <= quantile(claim_severity, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)) |>

  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +

  theme_minimal()









Observation: Comprehensive policies (COMP_E and COMP_N) show substantially higher claim severity compared to basic coverage types, reflecting their broader protection against more costly events like theft and total loss. The CC policies show moderate severity, consistent with covering multiple but selected risks. High variance within each policy type highlights the difficulty of predicting individual claim costs — a key driver of underwriting risk.

Island municipalities exhibit the highest urban claim frequencies, potentially reflecting road infrastructure differences. Coastal urban areas also show elevated frequencies. This geographic segmentation demonstrates that both location type and circulation environment are meaningful predictors of claim volatility.



7.2 Loss Ratio Over Time (Year)


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0) |>
  group_by(year, policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_lr, colour = policy_type, group = policy_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2022, 2023, 2024)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Mean Loss Ratio by Policy Type Over Time (2022–2024)",
       x = "Year", y = "Mean Loss Ratio", colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Loss ratios show variation across years and policy types. Any consistent upward trend across multiple policy types could indicate inflationary pressure on claims costs (e.g., rising repair costs or medical expenses), which is a key profitability concern for insurers. Policy types with consistently high loss ratios across years warrant closer underwriting scrutiny.



7.3 Relationship Between Premium and Incurred Cost


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0, total_premium > 0) |>
  filter(total_premium <= quantile(total_premium, 0.99),
         total_incurred <= quantile(total_incurred, 0.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium, y = total_incurred, colour = policy_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "red", 
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Premium vs Incurred Cost (Policies with Claims)",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = break-even (premium = incurred cost)",
       x = "Total Premium (€)", y = "Total Incurred (€)",
       colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2)))









Observation: Most policies with claims fall below the break-even line (incurred < premium), indicating individual profitability on these transactions. However, a notable cluster of policies exceed the break-even line, representing loss-making contracts. These tend to be clustered among comprehensive policies (COMP_E, COMP_N) with higher premiums, confirming that the wider coverage generates both higher revenue and higher claims exposure. The scatter reveals no strong linear relationship between premium and incurred cost, consistent with the inherent unpredictability of insurance claims.

8 Summary and Conclusion
This analysis explored the motor vehicle insurance portfolio across 354,140 policies spanning 2022–2024 using univariate and bivariate EDA methods.
Key findings on profitability:

The portfolio is dominated by CC and COMP_E policy types which carry the highest claim severity
Bonus score (claims history) is a strong predictor of loss ratio — “Bad” policyholders show markedly higher and more variable loss ratios
Comprehensive policies (COMP_E, COMP_N) consistently exhibit higher loss ratios than basic coverage types
Most policies (75%+) generate zero claims, creating a highly skewed loss distribution that drives average loss ratios

Key findings on volatility:

Young drivers (19–25) and urban circulation show the highest claim frequencies
Vehicle age, municipality type and circulation area all contribute to claim frequency variation
The heavy right tail in both claim frequency and severity distributions is the primary source of portfolio volatility
Island municipalities with urban circulation show the highest volatility signal

This presentation covers the visual analytics findings from a Spanish motor vehicle insurance portfolio containing 354,140 policy transactions from 2022 to 2024. We explore what drives profitability and volatility using exploratory data analysis with ggplot2. The analysis is structured in four parts: dataset overview, portfolio composition, profitability analysis, and volatility analysis.

About the Dataset


Source: Spanish motor insurer microdata
Period: January 2022 – December 2024
Records: 354,140 policy transactions
Variables: 47 across 4 groups

Three derived metrics guide analysis:
\[\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Premium}}\]
\[\text{Claim Freq} = \frac{\text{Claims}}{\text{Exposure}}\]
\[\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Claims}}\]






Note


Loss Ratio < 1 = Profitable
Loss Ratio > 1 = Unprofitable





The dataset is a real-world anonymised microdata portfolio from a Spanish motor insurer. Each row is a policy transaction. The key derived metrics we use throughout are the loss ratio as the profitability measure, claim frequency as the volatility measure, and claim severity as the average cost per claim. A loss ratio below 1 means premiums exceed claims — profitable. Above 1 means the insurer paid out more than it collected.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Data Quality


The dataset is exceptionally clean — only two variables have missing values. Fuel type is missing for about 0.37% of records and vehicle value for 0.10%. These missing values are handled by exclusion when those specific variables are analysed rather than imputed. All 47 variables have no structural issues and all categorical levels match the data dictionary exactly.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Policy Type & Status


The portfolio is dominated by CC policies at 62% — third-party liability combined with multiple additional coverages. Comprehensive policies with excess make up 22%. Basic third-party only policies are less than 1%, suggesting an above-average risk appetite from policyholders. About 85% of policies are active and 15% cancelled. A 15% cancellation rate is worth monitoring as cancelled policies may indicate adverse selection if higher-risk customers cancel after filing claims.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Driver & Vehicle Profile


The driver age distribution is centred around 45 to 55 years, indicating a portfolio dominated by experienced, middle-aged drivers. Very few young drivers under 25 appear, likely reflecting higher premiums that deter this segment. Vehicle age is right-skewed with many vehicles over 15 years old. Vehicle values cluster between 15,000 and 40,000 euros but have a long tail of high-value vehicles that can generate large claims when lost or damaged.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Geographic Distribution


The geographic spread is fairly balanced. Inland municipalities account for 54% with coastal at 36% and islands at 10%, broadly reflecting Spain’s population geography. Urban and rural circulation are nearly evenly split at 51 and 49 percent respectively. The bonus score distribution is striking — 98% of policyholders have a Good score, meaning excellent claims history. This is very positive for the portfolio but also means the Bad and Neutral segments are too small to draw strong statistical conclusions from.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio Overview


The loss ratio distribution is dominated by zero values — policies with no claims. Over three-quarters of policies have a loss ratio of zero. The mean loss ratio is substantially higher than the median due to a small number of very high-cost claims pulling the average up. Only a small percentage of policies have a loss ratio exceeding 1, but these loss-making policies disproportionately drive aggregate portfolio losses. The break-even line at LR equals 1 is the critical reference point.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio by Policy Type


Comprehensive policies — COMP_E and COMP_N — show the widest loss ratio distributions and highest medians, reflecting the broader coverage they provide. Basic TP and TPG policies have narrow distributions concentrated near zero. CC policies fall in the middle. This confirms that policy type is a primary driver of profitability: more comprehensive coverage equals higher loss ratio risk, which must be reflected in premium pricing.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio by Bonus Score


This is one of the strongest profitability signals in the dataset. Policyholders with a Bad bonus score — indicating prior claims — show markedly higher median loss ratios and much greater variance compared to Good-score policyholders. This validates the bonus-malus system as an effective risk differentiation tool. The Bad group, despite being less than 1% of the portfolio, contributes disproportionately to aggregate losses and volatility.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Claim Severity by Policy Type


Comprehensive policies generate not only more frequent claims but also more severe ones. COMP_E and COMP_N show the highest and most variable claim severity. This is expected since comprehensive policies cover events like theft and total loss which are costly. The wide interquartile range across all policy types highlights the difficulty of predicting individual claim costs — this unpredictability is the core source of underwriting risk.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Claim Frequency by Driver Age


Claim frequency follows the well-known U-shaped pattern by driver age. The youngest group from 19 to 25 shows the highest claim frequency due to inexperience. Frequency drops for middle-aged drivers from 35 to 55 who are the most experienced and safest. It then rises slightly for drivers over 65, possibly due to slower reaction times. This pattern is a classic actuarial finding and directly justifies age-based premium differentiation. The near-absence of under-25 drivers in this portfolio limits analysis of the youngest segment.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Claim Frequency by Geography


Urban circulation consistently drives higher claim frequencies across all municipality types, which makes intuitive sense given higher traffic density and accident exposure in urban environments. Island municipalities show the highest urban claim frequencies, possibly reflecting infrastructure limitations or road conditions. Coastal urban areas also show elevated frequencies. These geographic patterns suggest that both municipality type and circulation area should be used together as risk factors in pricing models.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio Trend Over Time


Tracking loss ratios over the three years reveals temporal patterns in profitability. Policy types that show an increasing trend may be experiencing claims inflation — rising repair or medical costs eating into margins. Comprehensive policies with their broader coverage are most exposed to such inflation. Stable or declining trends indicate effective pricing adjustments. Any divergence between policy types over time highlights segments that may need re-pricing in the next renewal cycle.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Key Findings Summary


Profitability Drivers

🔴 Bonus Score — Bad-score holders have significantly higher loss ratios
🔴 Policy Type — COMP_E/COMP_N carry the highest loss ratios
🟡 Vehicle Value — High-value vehicles generate higher severity
🟢 Portfolio Policies — Lower loss ratios vs new business


Volatility Drivers

🔴 Urban Circulation — Consistently higher claim frequency
🔴 Young Drivers — Highest frequency in 19–25 group
🟡 Islands — Elevated urban claim frequency
🟢 Good Bonus Score — Lowest frequency and variance








Important


75%+ of policies have zero claims — loss distribution is heavily right-skewed. A small fraction of policies drive the majority of portfolio losses.




To summarise the key findings: on profitability, bonus score and policy type are the two strongest drivers. Bad-score policyholders and comprehensive policy types consistently show higher loss ratios. On volatility, urban circulation and young driver age are the most significant factors. The overarching finding is that more than 75% of policies generate no claims at all — the portfolio’s profitability challenge comes entirely from a small number of high-cost policies. Managing these tail risks through better underwriting and pricing is the central challenge.
